stem: A 58-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history undergoes bronchoscopy for a chronic cough. Biopsy of the main bronchus shows stratified squamous epithelium replacing the normal pseudostratified ciliated columnar lining, with no nuclear atypia. Which statement best describes this change?
options: It is a reversible adaptive change caused by reprogramming of reserve (stem) cells, and persistent exposure predisposes to dysplasia and carcinoma
It is an irreversible change caused by direct transformation of mature ciliated cells into squamous cells
It represents an increase in the number of cells of the normal bronchial epithelium due to a hormonal stimulus
It is a disordered, atypical proliferation of epithelium that is already a pre-invasive carcinoma
It is a loss of differentiation with pleomorphism that is the hallmark of malignancy
explanation: Metaplasia is a reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another that is better able to withstand stress (here, chronic smoke exposure). It results from reprogramming of reserve/stem cells, and if the stimulus persists it can progress to dysplasia and then carcinoma. (First Aid — Pathology: Cellular adaptations)
optionExplanations: Metaplasia arises from reprogramming of stem/reserve cells, not from mature cells transdifferentiating, and it is reversible if the stimulus is removed.
That describes hyperplasia, in which the cell type is unchanged.
Atypia and disordered maturation define dysplasia; the biopsy here shows none.
Loss of differentiation (anaplasia) is a feature of cancer, not of benign metaplasia.

stem: A 55-year-old man with stage 5 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 12 mL/min) has fatigue and pallor. Hb is 7.8 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, reticulocyte count is low, and serum ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal. What is the principal mechanism of his anaemia?
options: Impaired iron absorption due to uraemic gastritis
Reduced erythropoietin production by peritubular interstitial cells of the damaged kidney
Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells with intrinsic factor deficiency
Increased intravascular haemolysis from uraemic toxins
Marrow replacement by fibrosis due to secondary hyperparathyroidism
explanation: Anaemia of CKD is normocytic and normochromic with a low reticulocyte count and normal iron stores. The cause is decreased erythropoietin synthesis by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts, and it is treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents once iron stores are replete. (First Aid — Renal: Chronic kidney disease)
optionExplanations: Iron studies are normal, so iron deficiency is not the main mechanism.
That causes a macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia, not a normocytic one.
Haemolysis would produce a raised, not low, reticulocyte count.
Marrow fibrosis can contribute minimally but is not the principal mechanism of CKD anaemia.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing chronic kidney disease and persistent anaemia is under review. Which set of laboratory findings is most typical of her anaemia?
options: Microcytic hypochromic indices, low ferritin, high TIBC
Normocytic normochromic indices, low reticulocyte count, normal ferritin and transferrin saturation
Normocytic indices, high ferritin, low TIBC and low serum iron
Microcytic indices with high serum iron and ringed sideroblasts
explanation: The anaemia of CKD results from erythropoietin deficiency, so the red cells are normocytic and normochromic, reticulocytes are low, and iron indices are normal unless there is coexisting iron deficiency. Anaemia of chronic inflammation shows a high ferritin with low iron and TIBC, which is the main distractor. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Anemias)
optionExplanations: This is the pattern of iron deficiency anaemia.
This is the pattern of megaloblastic anaemia from B12 or folate deficiency.
This describes anaemia of chronic inflammation, which is not the primary mechanism of CKD anaemia.
This describes sideroblastic anaemia.

stem: Which cytokine axis is most critical for macrophage activation and granuloma formation in response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
options: IL-4 from Th2 cells driving IgE class switching
IL-17 from Th17 cells recruiting neutrophils
IL-10 from regulatory T cells suppressing macrophages
IL-12 from infected macrophages driving Th1 cells to secrete IFN-gamma
IL-5 from Th2 cells recruiting eosinophils
explanation: Infected macrophages release IL-12, which drives CD4 T cells toward the Th1 subset. Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages to kill mycobacteria and to form epithelioid cells and granulomas. Defects in IL-12 or IFN-gamma signalling cause disseminated mycobacterial disease. (First Aid — Immunology: Cytokines; Microbiology: Mycobacteria)
optionExplanations: IL-4/Th2 responses mediate allergic and anti-helminth immunity, not control of intracellular mycobacteria.
Th17 cells defend against extracellular bacteria and fungi and do not drive the main anti-mycobacterial macrophage activation.
IL-10 dampens macrophage activity and would impair granuloma formation.
IL-5 stimulates eosinophils and is not involved in granuloma formation against TB.

stem: Lung biopsy of a patient with pulmonary tuberculosis shows granulomas with central caseous necrosis surrounded by epithelioid macrophages. Many multinucleated giant cells have their nuclei arranged in a horseshoe pattern at the periphery of the cell. These cells are best described as:
options: Touton giant cells containing a ring of nuclei around a central core of lipid
Foreign-body giant cells with randomly scattered nuclei
Warthin-Finkeldey cells found in lymphoid tissue
Langhans giant cells formed by fusion of epithelioid macrophages
explanation: Langhans giant cells result from fusion of epithelioid macrophages in granulomas and have nuclei arranged peripherally in a horseshoe or ring pattern. They are typical of tuberculous granulomas, but are not specific to TB. (First Aid — Pathology: Inflammation; Microbiology: Mycobacteria)
optionExplanations: Touton cells have a wreath of nuclei around a central homogeneous core and are seen in lipid-rich lesions such as xanthomas.
Foreign-body cells have haphazardly arranged nuclei and form around inert material such as sutures.
These are multinucleated giant cells of measles infection, not of TB granuloma.
Reed-Sternberg cells are binucleate neoplastic cells of Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: A 45-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has been started on infliximab. Six months later he develops fever, weight loss, and an upper-lobe cavitary lesion; biopsy shows reactivated tuberculosis with poorly formed granulomas. Which mediator, now blocked, is required for maintaining granuloma integrity?
explanation: TNF-alpha, produced by activated macrophages, is essential for recruiting and retaining cells within granulomas. Anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab can therefore allow reactivation of latent TB, which is why patients are screened for latent TB before starting them. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Immunosuppressants; Immunology: Cytokines)
optionExplanations: IL-4 is a Th2 cytokine and is not required for maintaining anti-mycobacterial granulomas.
TGF-beta promotes fibrosis and immunosuppression and is not the mediator blocked by infliximab.
IL-2 supports T-cell proliferation but is not the target of infliximab.
G-CSF stimulates neutrophil production and is not the target of infliximab.

stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with polyuria, weight loss, and ketoacidosis. Islet histology at autopsy of a similar case shows lymphocytic infiltration of the islets (insulitis) with selective loss of beta cells. Which type of hypersensitivity is the principal mechanism of beta-cell destruction?
options: Type II (antibody mediated against cell-surface antigens)
explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which CD8 and CD4 T cells infiltrate the islets (insulitis) and destroy beta cells, which is classified as type IV hypersensitivity. Islet autoantibodies such as anti-GAD65 are useful markers but are not the main effector. (First Aid — Immunology: Hypersensitivity; Endocrine: Diabetes mellitus)
optionExplanations: Type I reactions involve IgE and mast-cell degranulation and are seen in allergy and anaphylaxis.
Autoantibodies are markers of type 1 diabetes but the destruction of beta cells is chiefly T-cell mediated.
Immune-complex deposition causes serum sickness and SLE nephritis, not insulitis.
Receptor-stimulating antibodies are seen in Graves disease, and this category is not a standard type in First Aid.

stem: A lean 16-year-old girl is found to have mild persistent hyperglycaemia (fasting glucose 8.2 mmol/L) at a school screening. She has never had ketoacidosis and is not on insulin. Her mother, maternal uncle, and grandmother were all diagnosed with diabetes before age 30. Islet autoantibodies (anti-GAD, IA-2) are negative and C-peptide is preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: MODY is an autosomal dominant monogenic form of diabetes (for example HNF1A or glucokinase mutations) presenting in lean young people with a strong multigenerational family history, negative autoantibodies and preserved C-peptide. It is non-ketotic and often responds to sulfonylureas. (First Aid — Endocrine: Diabetes mellitus)
optionExplanations: Type 1 diabetes presents with ketosis, insulin dependence, low C-peptide and positive islet autoantibodies.
LADA occurs in adults with positive GAD antibodies and progressive beta-cell failure, which does not fit this adolescent with negative antibodies.
Type 2 diabetes is typically associated with obesity and insulin resistance, and a three-generation dominant pattern at young age points to a monogenic form.
She is not pregnant, and this is a persistent non-gestational hyperglycaemia.

stem: A 38-year-old lean man was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and initially controlled his glucose with oral agents. Within 18 months he is losing weight, develops ketosis, and no longer responds to sulfonylureas. Anti-GAD65 antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Classic type 2 diabetes with secondary sulfonylurea failure
explanation: LADA is a slowly progressive form of autoimmune (type 1-like) diabetes in adults that is initially mistaken for type 2 diabetes. Clues are leanness, GAD antibodies, and early failure of oral agents with progression to insulin dependence. (First Aid — Endocrine: Diabetes mellitus)
optionExplanations: MODY is antibody negative and does not progress to insulin dependence.
Positive GAD antibodies with leanness and rapid beta-cell failure indicate an autoimmune process.
There is no history of pancreatic disease, and GAD antibodies would not be positive.
Cushing syndrome causes insulin resistance, with central obesity, not autoimmune beta-cell failure.

stem: A 22-year-old man has had a splenectomy after a road traffic accident. A peripheral blood film now shows erythrocytes containing small, round, basophilic nuclear remnants. These inclusions are best identified as:
explanation: Howell-Jolly bodies are DNA (nuclear) remnants in red cells that are normally removed by splenic macrophages, so they appear after splenectomy or in functional asplenia such as sickle cell disease. Patients need vaccination against encapsulated organisms. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: RBC morphology)
optionExplanations: Heinz bodies are denatured haemoglobin seen with supravital stain in G6PD deficiency.
Basophilic stippling is multiple fine granules of ribosomal precipitates seen in lead poisoning and thalassaemia.
Pappenheimer bodies are iron-containing granules seen in sideroblastic anaemia.
Cabot rings are ring-shaped remnants of the mitotic spindle seen in megaloblastic anaemia and lead poisoning.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue and pallor. Which laboratory pattern is expected in iron deficiency anaemia?
options: Low serum ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC and low transferrin saturation
High serum ferritin, low serum iron, low TIBC and low transferrin saturation
Normal ferritin, normal iron and normal TIBC with microcytosis
High serum ferritin, high serum iron, normal TIBC and high transferrin saturation
Low serum ferritin, high serum iron and high transferrin saturation
explanation: In iron deficiency, depleted stores give a low ferritin (the most specific test), low serum iron and transferrin saturation, and a compensatory increase in TIBC (transferrin). Red cells are microcytic and hypochromic with an increased RDW. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Iron deficiency anemia)
optionExplanations: This is the pattern of anaemia of chronic disease.
This pattern is seen in thalassaemia trait where iron stores are normal.
This is the iron-overloaded pattern of sideroblastic anaemia or haemochromatosis.
Low ferritin indicates depleted stores, so iron and saturation would be low.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with fatigue. Hb is 8.4 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, and ferritin is 6 ng/mL. He has no history of dietary deficiency or blood donation. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start oral ferrous sulphate and review in 3 months
Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy to look for a bleeding source
explanation: Iron deficiency in an adult man or postmenopausal woman is considered to be due to gastrointestinal blood loss, including colorectal cancer, until proven otherwise. Endoscopy is needed in addition to iron replacement. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Iron deficiency anemia)
optionExplanations: Treating without finding the cause could miss a gastrointestinal malignancy in this age group.
Marrow examination is not needed when ferritin is clearly low and the cause is probably occult blood loss.
Electrophoresis is for suspected thalassaemia, in which ferritin is normal, not low.
B12 and folate deficiency cause macrocytosis, not microcytosis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has fatigue, glossitis, and tingling paraesthesia in her feet. Hb is 7.9 g/dL, MCV 119 fL, and the film shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Her serum methylmalonic acid is markedly raised. Which cause is most likely?
options: Vitamin B12 deficiency from autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia)
explanation: Raised methylmalonic acid with macrocytic anaemia and neurological signs indicates B12 deficiency, since methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs B12 while folate deficiency spares it. Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor, with B12 absorption failing in the terminal ileum. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Megaloblastic anemias)
optionExplanations: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia with raised homocysteine but normal methylmalonic acid, and no neuropathy.
Iron deficiency gives a microcytic anaemia.
CKD gives a normocytic anaemia and does not raise methylmalonic acid or cause macrocytosis.
MDS may be macrocytic but does not explain the raised methylmalonic acid or dorsal-column neuropathy.

stem: Which defect underlies the characteristic bone marrow findings of megaloblastic anaemia?
options: Impaired haem synthesis from deficient delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase activity
Impaired synthesis of both DNA and RNA with a hypocellular marrow
Impaired DNA synthesis (thymidylate and purine synthesis) with preserved RNA and protein synthesis, causing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony
Increased peripheral destruction of normal red cells
explanation: Deficiency of folate or B12 impairs thymidylate and purine synthesis, so DNA replication lags while RNA and cytoplasmic maturation continue. The result is large cells with immature nuclei (nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony), ineffective erythropoiesis and macro-ovalocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Megaloblastic anemias)
optionExplanations: This defect causes sideroblastic anaemia, not megaloblastic changes.
This defect underlies the thalassaemias.
Megaloblastic marrow is hypercellular with ineffective erythropoiesis, and RNA/protein synthesis is preserved.
Megaloblastic anaemia is due to ineffective erythropoiesis in the marrow, not primarily peripheral destruction.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with breast cancer receives a cumulative high dose of an anthracycline. Months later she develops dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and an echocardiogram shows a dilated, hypokinetic left ventricle. Which drug is the most likely cause, and which agent can reduce this toxicity?
explanation: Doxorubicin and daunorubicin cause dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy through free-radical damage to cardiomyocytes. Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, is cardioprotective. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Antineoplastic drugs)
optionExplanations: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis, and amifostine protects against cisplatin nephrotoxicity.
Cisplatin causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, and mesna is used for cyclophosphamide haemorrhagic cystitis.
Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy, and leucovorin rescues from methotrexate.
Methotrexate causes myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity rather than dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 64-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has taken amiodarone for 8 months. He now has progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. Chest examination reveals bibasal crackles, and chest X-ray shows reticular interstitial shadowing. PFTs show a restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO. Which adverse effect of amiodarone does this represent?
explanation: Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis leading to fibrosis) presents with dyspnoea, cough and restrictive PFTs with reduced DLCO. Baseline and periodic PFTs, TFTs and LFTs are needed, and other effects include thyroid dysfunction, corneal deposits, blue-grey skin and photosensitivity. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Antiarrhythmics, class III)
optionExplanations: Thyroid dysfunction would give fatigue and cold intolerance and would not cause restrictive lung disease.
Corneal deposits are common and benign and do not cause respiratory symptoms.
Amiodarone can cause hepatotoxicity but not interstitial lung shadowing.
This is a prolonged-QT arrhythmia and does not cause a restrictive lung pattern.

stem: A 60-year-old woman on long-term amiodarone is found to have fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and a raised TSH. Which statement best explains why amiodarone can cause this?
options: Amiodarone causes autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells
The high iodine load of amiodarone inhibits thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect), and it also blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
Amiodarone induces anti-TSH receptor stimulating antibodies
Amiodarone blocks beta receptors and lowers basal metabolic rate
explanation: Amiodarone is about 37% iodine by weight and can suppress thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) and inhibit deiodination of T4 to T3, leading to hypothyroidism. It can also cause hyperthyroidism, so TFTs are monitored. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Antiarrhythmics, class III)
optionExplanations: Amiodarone-induced hypothyroidism is not mainly autoimmune.
Stimulating antibodies cause Graves hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.
Beta blockade is a property of amiodarone but it does not lead to a raised TSH.
Altered TBG does not produce a raised TSH with hypothyroid symptoms.

stem: A 9-year-old boy with a long-standing congenital heart lesion has cyanosis and clubbing. His ECG shows a mean frontal QRS axis of +120 degrees, a tall R wave in V1, and a deep S wave in V6. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Left ventricular hypertrophy with left axis deviation
Right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation
explanation: A QRS axis between +90 and +180 degrees is right axis deviation, and with a dominant R in V1 and an S in V6 it indicates right ventricular hypertrophy. Causes include pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary stenosis, and Eisenmenger physiology. (First Aid — Cardiovascular: ECG)
optionExplanations: LVH produces a leftward axis with a tall R in V5-V6 and deep S in V1.
LAFB causes marked left axis deviation (beyond -45 degrees).
An axis of +120 degrees is beyond the normal adult range of -30 to +90 degrees and indicates right axis deviation.
LBBB causes a broad QRS with a leftward axis and a QS or rS pattern in V1.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with orthopnoea, ankle swelling, and elevated JVP. A blood marker is requested to support the diagnosis of congestive cardiac failure. Which marker is most specific for this condition?
explanation: BNP is released by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stretch and volume overload. It is raised in heart failure, with a high negative predictive value for excluding it, whereas troponin and CK-MB reflect myocyte necrosis. (First Aid — Cardiovascular: Heart failure)
optionExplanations: Troponin is a marker of myocardial necrosis and is not specific for heart failure.
CK-MB is an older marker of myocardial injury.
LDH is non-specific and is released from many tissues.
Myoglobin rises early after muscle or myocardial injury but is not specific for heart failure.

stem: Twelve hours after a family dinner that included fried rice cooked the previous day and left at room temperature, several members develop profuse watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramps without fever. Which organism is the most likely cause?
explanation: Bacillus cereus causes food poisoning from reheated rice. Its emetic form (heat-stable preformed toxin) causes vomiting 1-5 hours after ingestion, while the diarrhoeal form causes watery diarrhoea 8-18 hours later. Spores survive cooking and germinate when rice is left at room temperature. (First Aid — Microbiology: Bacillus cereus)
optionExplanations: C. perfringens also causes watery diarrhoea at 8-16 hours but is classically linked to reheated meat dishes and gravies.
S. aureus produces a preformed toxin and causes predominant vomiting within 1-6 hours.
Salmonella typically causes fever and is linked to poultry and eggs.
This is linked to raw or undercooked seafood.

stem: A 9-year-old girl with pharyngitis has a throat swab cultured on sheep blood agar. Colonies show a clear zone of complete haemolysis, are catalase negative, and show a zone of inhibition around a bacitracin disc. Which organism is most likely?
explanation: Group A streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is beta-haemolytic, bacitracin sensitive and PYR positive, and is catalase negative. Group B streptococcus is bacitracin resistant with a positive CAMP test and hippurate hydrolysis. (First Aid — Microbiology: Streptococci)
optionExplanations: Group B streptococci are also beta-haemolytic but are bacitracin resistant and CAMP test positive.
S. pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic (partial haemolysis with green discolouration) and optochin sensitive.
These are alpha-haemolytic and optochin resistant.
S. aureus is catalase positive and coagulase positive.

stem: An alpha-haemolytic, catalase-negative, gram-positive diplococcus is isolated from the sputum of a patient with lobar pneumonia. Which test best distinguishes this organism from viridans streptococci?
options: Sensitivity to optochin and solubility in bile
Growth in 6.5% NaCl and bile esculin hydrolysis
explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococcus that is optochin sensitive and bile soluble, whereas viridans streptococci are optochin resistant and bile insoluble. (First Aid — Microbiology: Streptococci)
optionExplanations: Bacitracin sensitivity separates group A from group B beta-haemolytic streptococci.
The CAMP test identifies group B streptococci.
These tests identify Enterococcus.
Coagulase identifies Staphylococcus aureus.

stem: A 46-year-old man hospitalised with pneumonia has a total leucocyte count of 62 x 10^9/L with neutrophilia, left shift including metamyelocytes and myelocytes, toxic granulation, and a high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score. BCR-ABL testing is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A leukemoid reaction is a reactive neutrophilia with a left shift in response to infection or inflammation, and it shows toxic granulation and a high LAP score. CML is distinguished by a low LAP score, BCR-ABL positivity and basophilia. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Myeloproliferative disorders)
optionExplanations: CML has a low LAP score and is BCR-ABL positive, with basophilia.
AML has circulating blasts with a typically anaemic and thrombocytopenic picture.
CLL shows mature lymphocytosis with smudge cells.
PV is a JAK2-mutated erythrocytosis, whereas this patient has an isolated neutrophilic leucocytosis.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has a photosensitive malar rash, recurrent abdominal pain, and low mood. She is found to have proteinuria. Which antibody is most specific for her probable diagnosis and correlates with disease activity and lupus nephritis?
explanation: The clinical picture suggests SLE with multi-system involvement, including neuropsychiatric features. ANA is sensitive but not specific, whereas anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are specific, and anti-dsDNA titres track disease activity and lupus nephritis. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal: SLE)
optionExplanations: ANA is the most sensitive screening test but has low specificity.
Anti-histone antibodies are characteristic of drug-induced lupus.
Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST).
Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are associated with polymyositis and dermatomyositis.

stem: A 60-year-old man has haematuria, flank pain, and a palpable mass. CT shows an 8 cm renal mass, and biopsy shows polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm arranged in nests. Which genetic abnormality is most characteristic of this tumour?
options: Mutation of the WT1 gene on chromosome 11p
Loss of function of the Rb gene on chromosome 13q
Inactivation of the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p
explanation: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is associated with VHL gene loss on chromosome 3p in both sporadic and von Hippel-Lindau-associated cases. Loss of VHL leads to stabilisation of HIF, which upregulates VEGF and PDGF. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Tumor suppressor genes; Renal: Renal cell carcinoma)
optionExplanations: WT1 mutations are associated with Wilms tumour in children.
N-myc amplification is a poor prognostic marker in neuroblastoma.
RET mutations occur in MEN2 and papillary or medullary thyroid cancer.
Rb loss causes retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma.

stem: A 62-year-old smoker with a renal mass has a haemoglobin of 19 g/dL and a raised haematocrit with no hypoxia. Which substance is most likely secreted by his tumour?
explanation: Renal cell carcinoma can produce paraneoplastic syndromes such as erythropoietin secretion (polycythaemia), PTHrP (hypercalcaemia), renin and ACTH. It spreads via the renal vein, with cannonball metastases to the lungs. (First Aid — Renal: Renal cell carcinoma)
optionExplanations: True PTH secretion by RCC is rare, and PTH-related peptide would cause hypercalcaemia, not polycythaemia.
ADH secretion would cause hyponatraemia, not polycythaemia.
This would raise platelet count, not haemoglobin.
IGF-2 secretion is associated with hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 52-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has mildly raised ALT on routine testing. Liver biopsy shows hepatocytes with large clear vacuoles that displace the nucleus to the periphery. Viral serology is negative. What do these vacuoles contain?
explanation: Large vacuoles that push the nucleus aside are macrovesicular fat (triglyceride) in hepatocytes. The vacuoles are empty on routine H&E because the lipid is dissolved during processing, and they are shown by Oil red O staining on frozen sections. This is typical of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease with metabolic syndrome. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Hepatic disease)
optionExplanations: Glycogenosis produces clear hepatocytes that are PAS positive and diastase sensitive, but the clinical setting here is metabolic.
Hydropic swelling produces ballooned cells with a granular cytoplasm and no discrete large vacuoles displacing the nucleus.
Haemosiderin appears as golden-brown granules (Prussian blue positive).
Bile pigment causes yellow-green canalicular plugs.

stem: In a rural area, a 45-year-old man whose diet consists almost entirely of maize (corn) presents with a photosensitive scaly dermatitis on the neck and hands, chronic diarrhoea, and memory loss. Which deficiency is responsible?
explanation: Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia) results from niacin deficiency. Maize contains niacin in a bound, unavailable form and is low in tryptophan, which is the precursor of niacin. Other causes include Hartnup disease and carcinoid syndrome. (First Aid — Biochemistry: Vitamins)
optionExplanations: Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
Riboflavin deficiency causes cheilosis, angular stomatitis and corneal vascularisation.
B6 deficiency causes convulsions, hyperirritability and sideroblastic anaemia.
B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration.

stem: A 30-year-old multiparous woman delivers a macrosomic infant after a prolonged labour augmented with oxytocin. Thirty minutes later she is bleeding heavily, and on examination the uterus is soft, boggy, and above the umbilicus. The placenta is complete and there are no genital tract lacerations. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage (the 'tone' of the four Ts), and risk factors include prolonged labour, macrosomia, oxytocin use, and multiparity. It presents with a soft, boggy uterus, and is managed with fundal massage, oxytocin and other uterotonics. (First Aid — Reproductive: Postpartum hemorrhage)
optionExplanations: The placenta is complete, and retained tissue would also tend to leave a firm or partially contracted uterus.
Lacerations cause bleeding with a well-contracted uterus.
Inversion causes a mass at the introitus and an absent fundus with shock.
DIC causes bleeding from multiple sites with a coagulopathy, which is not indicated here.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 36 weeks of gestation has a placental abruption and delivers a stillborn infant. She then develops oozing from venepuncture sites and heavy vaginal bleeding. Which laboratory profile is expected?
options: Normal PT and aPTT, low platelets, normal fibrinogen
Prolonged aPTT only, with normal PT, platelets, and fibrinogen
Prolonged bleeding time with normal PT and aPTT, platelets normal
Prolonged PT with normal aPTT and raised fibrinogen
Prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, low platelets, raised D-dimer
explanation: Placental abruption releases tissue factor and triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation. Consumption of clotting factors and platelets gives prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia, and markedly raised D-dimer, with schistocytes on the film. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Disseminated intravascular coagulation)
optionExplanations: This describes isolated thrombocytopenia and does not match DIC.
This is seen in haemophilia or heparin therapy.
This is seen in von Willebrand disease or platelet function defects.
This points to early vitamin K deficiency or warfarin, and fibrinogen would not be raised.

stem: A woman with severe postpartum haemorrhage has been resuscitated with crystalloid and packed red cells. Her fibrinogen is 1.0 g/L and bleeding continues. Which blood product is the most appropriate source of fibrinogen to correct this?
explanation: Fibrinogen falls early in obstetric haemorrhage and DIC, and low levels predict severe bleeding. Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII, and von Willebrand factor, and is the preferred product to replace fibrinogen. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Transfusion products)
optionExplanations: These carry oxygen and contain no meaningful quantity of fibrinogen.
Platelets replace platelet number and do not supply fibrinogen.
Albumin is a volume expander and not a source of clotting factors.
Crystalloids dilute clotting factors further.

stem: A 5-month-old boy has developmental regression, seizures, hypotonia, and sparse, hypopigmented, brittle ('kinky') hair. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low. Which biochemical defect is responsible?
explanation: Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive defect in the ATP7A copper-transporting ATPase, which impairs intestinal copper absorption and delivery to tissues. Low copper-dependent enzyme activity (for example lysyl oxidase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase) causes kinky hair, neurodegeneration, and connective tissue defects. (First Aid — Biochemistry: Menkes disease)
optionExplanations: Iron absorption defects cause microcytic anaemia, not kinky hair and neurodegeneration.
Impaired zinc absorption causes acrodermatitis enteropathica, with perioral rash, alopecia, and diarrhoea.
Wilson disease (ATP7B) impairs copper excretion and incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and presents later with liver and basal ganglia disease.
Selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease), not this syndrome.

stem: Bupivacaine is infiltrated before a surgical incision. Which statement correctly describes its mechanism of action?
options: It blocks voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic terminal
It opens voltage-gated potassium channels to hyperpolarise the axon
It blocks voltage-gated sodium channels from the intracellular side, preferentially in the open and inactivated state
It blocks sodium channels from the extracellular side in the resting state
explanation: Local anaesthetics such as bupivacaine block voltage-gated sodium channels from within the axoplasm after diffusing through the membrane. They bind preferentially to open/inactivated channels, so rapidly firing, smaller fibres are blocked first (use-dependent block). (First Aid — Pharmacology: Local anesthetics)
optionExplanations: Calcium channel blockade is not the mechanism of local anaesthetics.
Local anaesthetics do not open potassium channels.
This is the mechanism of benzodiazepines and barbiturates (GABA-A).
Local anaesthetics cross the membrane in the uncharged form and act from inside, with greater affinity for open or inactivated channels.

stem: A 3-week-old term infant has a high-pitched inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine and during feeding, and improves in the prone position. He is thriving. Flexible laryngoscopy shows an omega-shaped epiglottis with collapse of the aryepiglottic folds into the airway on inspiration. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Laryngomalacia is the commonest cause of stridor in infants. Floppy supraglottic tissues (omega epiglottis, short aryepiglottic folds) collapse on inspiration, and it usually resolves by 12-18 months with conservative management. (First Aid — Respiratory: Pediatric upper airway)
optionExplanations: Subglottic stenosis gives a biphasic stridor and is not related to supraglottic collapse.
Cord paralysis presents with stridor and a weak cry, with immobile cords.
Tracheomalacia gives expiratory stridor or wheeze.
A web causes a hoarse or absent cry with biphasic stridor from birth.

stem: An 8-year-old boy has fever, sore throat, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudate without cough. A rapid antigen test is positive. Treatment of this infection with antibiotics is primarily aimed at preventing which complication?
explanation: Group A streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis is treated with penicillin primarily to prevent acute rheumatic fever. Treatment, even when delayed up to 9 days after onset, does not prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. (First Aid — Microbiology: Group A streptococci; Cardiovascular: Rheumatic fever)
optionExplanations: Antibiotic therapy does not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Scarlet fever is caused by pyrogenic exotoxin and is not the main reason to treat.
Endocarditis prophylaxis does not apply to uncomplicated pharyngitis.
Reye syndrome follows aspirin use during viral illness and is unrelated.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has chronic nasal obstruction with foul-smelling crusts, a very wide nasal cavity with atrophic turbinates, and loss of smell. Which organism is classically associated with this condition?
explanation: Primary atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) presents with foul crusts, atrophic mucosa, a roomy nasal cavity, and anosmia. Klebsiella ozaenae (Klebsiella pneumoniae subsp. ozaenae) is the organism most often isolated. (First Aid — Microbiology: Klebsiella)
optionExplanations: S. aureus causes nasal furuncles and vestibulitis.
H. influenzae is a cause of otitis media and sinusitis.
Pseudomonas is associated with malignant otitis externa.
Leprosy can cause nasal destruction, but the described features are those of primary atrophic rhinitis.

stem: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes and ketoacidosis presents with facial pain, periorbital swelling, and a black necrotic eschar on the nasal turbinate. Biopsy of the eschar is most likely to show which finding?
options: Septate hyphae branching at acute (45-degree) angles
Broad, ribbon-like, non-septate hyphae branching at right angles
Narrow-based budding yeast with a thick capsule
explanation: Rhinocerebral mucormycosis (Mucor, Rhizopus) occurs in diabetic ketoacidosis and neutropenia and causes black necrotic nasal tissue with orbital and brain extension. Hyphae are broad, non-septate and branch at right angles. Management is surgical debridement and liposomal amphotericin B. (First Aid — Microbiology: Mucor and Rhizopus)
optionExplanations: This describes Aspergillus.
This describes Candida.
This describes Cryptococcus.
This describes Coccidioides.

stem: After a head injury, a patient has clear watery fluid dripping from his nose. Which test is most specific for confirming that the fluid is cerebrospinal fluid?
options: Glucose content greater than 30 mg/dL in the fluid
explanation: Beta-2 transferrin (and beta-trace protein) is present almost exclusively in CSF, perilymph and vitreous humour, making it the most specific confirmatory test for CSF rhinorrhoea. Glucose and halo sign are unreliable. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Cerebrospinal fluid)
optionExplanations: Nasal secretions and tears also contain glucose, so this test is unreliable.
The halo sign is non-specific because blood-mixed mucus can produce the same sign.
This is not used for confirming CSF.
Culture shows microbial growth and cannot confirm CSF.

stem: Beta-2 transferrin has confirmed CSF rhinorrhoea in a patient with a previous skull-base fracture. Which imaging modality best demonstrates the bony skull-base defect?
options: High-resolution CT of the skull base (thin-cut coronal)
explanation: High-resolution thin-section CT is the investigation of choice to locate bony defects of the skull base in CSF leak. MRI cisternography can complement it to show soft-tissue herniation. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Skull base anatomy)
optionExplanations: Plain films have a low yield for identifying small skull-base defects.
Angiography demonstrates vascular, not bony, abnormalities.
Doppler ultrasound is for vascular flow assessment, not bony defect imaging.
This is unrelated to skull-base imaging.

stem: A 10-month-old infant develops vomiting and lethargy after a prolonged overnight fast during a viral illness. Blood glucose is 1.8 mmol/L, urine ketones are absent, and plasma free carnitine is low. Which metabolic pathway is most likely defective?
options: Ketone body utilisation in peripheral tissues
explanation: Fatty acid oxidation produces acetyl-CoA for ketogenesis and supplies energy during fasting. Defects in this pathway (for example MCAD deficiency or carnitine transport defects) cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting or illness. (First Aid — Biochemistry: Fatty acid oxidation disorders)
optionExplanations: Gluconeogenesis defects usually cause ketotic hypoglycaemia with lactic acidosis.
Glycogenolysis defects cause hepatomegaly and ketotic hypoglycaemia.
A utilisation defect would cause high ketones.
Urea cycle defects cause hyperammonaemia and respiratory alkalosis, not hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 28-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for testicular germ-cell tumour develops bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a rising creatinine. Which drug is most likely responsible?
explanation: Cisplatin causes ototoxicity (irreversible high-frequency sensorineural loss), nephrotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy. Hydration and amifostine can reduce renal toxicity. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Antineoplastic drugs)
optionExplanations: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy and not hearing loss.
Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis and skin toxicity.
Doxorubicin causes dilated cardiomyopathy.
Methotrexate causes myelosuppression and mucositis.

stem: A patient has right facial palsy with loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and loss of the stapedial reflex (hyperacusis), but tear production is normal. At which level is the facial nerve lesion?
options: Between the geniculate ganglion and the origin of the nerve to stapedius
Between the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani
explanation: Facial nerve branches arise in order: greater petrosal nerve (lacrimation) at the geniculate ganglion, nerve to stapedius, then chorda tympani (taste of anterior two-thirds of tongue). Normal lacrimation places the lesion distal to the geniculate ganglion, and loss of both the stapedial reflex and taste places it proximal to the nerve to stapedius. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Facial nerve)
optionExplanations: A lesion here would also abolish lacrimation, as the greater petrosal nerve fibres are affected.
A lesion at the geniculate ganglion would involve the greater petrosal nerve and reduce lacrimation.
The stapedial reflex would be preserved since the nerve to stapedius arises proximal to the lesion.
Only facial muscle paralysis would occur, with preserved taste, lacrimation and stapedius function.

stem: Which muscle of the middle ear inserts on the handle of the malleus, and what is its nerve supply?
options: Tensor tympani; mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
Stapedius; mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
explanation: Tensor tympani, derived from the first pharyngeal arch, inserts onto the handle of the malleus and is supplied by V3 (nerve to medial pterygoid). It dampens loud sounds, whereas stapedius is second-arch derived, inserts on the stapes and is supplied by the facial nerve. (First Aid — Anatomy: Pharyngeal arch derivatives)
optionExplanations: Stapedius inserts on the neck of the stapes and is supplied by the facial nerve.
Tensor tympani is supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid, a branch of V3, not the facial nerve.
Stapedius is derived from the second arch and supplied by the facial nerve.
Tensor veli palatini lies in the soft palate and is supplied by V3, not by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

stem: A 60-year-old man is treated with gentamicin for sepsis and develops tinnitus and bilateral high-frequency hearing loss. Which cochlear structure is damaged first?
options: Inner hair cells at the apical turn
Outer hair cells at the basal turn
explanation: Aminoglycosides accumulate in perilymph and endolymph and destroy hair cells, starting with the outer hair cells of the basal turn. This produces high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and the damage is irreversible. Loop diuretics affect the stria vascularis. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Aminoglycosides)
optionExplanations: Inner hair cells are more resistant, and the apex mediates low-frequency hearing.
The stria vascularis is the usual site of loop diuretic ototoxicity.
Neuronal degeneration is secondary and is not the first site of aminoglycoside damage.
This is not the primary target of aminoglycoside ototoxicity.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has brief episodes of spinning vertigo on turning over in bed. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre provokes torsional upbeat nystagmus after a few seconds' latency that fatigues. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Endolymphatic hydrops of the cochlear duct and saccule
Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
Displaced otoconia (canalithiasis) in the posterior semicircular canal
explanation: BPPV results from otoliths (canalithiasis) in the posterior semicircular canal, causing brief positional vertigo with latent, fatigable torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing. It is treated with canalith repositioning (Epley manoeuvre). (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Vertigo)
optionExplanations: This causes Meniere disease, with episodes lasting hours with hearing loss.
Vestibular neuritis causes acute persistent vertigo for days, not positional episodes.
A vestibular schwannoma causes progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus.
This would cause acute vertigo with associated deafness.

stem: A 45-year-old man has recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting 2-3 hours, associated with roaring tinnitus, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, and a feeling of fullness in the left ear. What is the underlying pathology?
options: Otoconial displacement in the posterior canal
explanation: Meniere disease features episodic vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. It results from excess endolymph (endolymphatic hydrops). (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Vertigo)
optionExplanations: A fistula typically follows trauma or barotrauma and causes vertigo on straining.
Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss, without vertigo episodes.
This produces brief, positional vertigo without hearing loss.
Schwannoma causes progressive unilateral sensorineural loss, with no episodic hours-long vertigo.

stem: In a study of a new vaccine, the investigators record whether each participant develops a thromboembolic event at each dose level and plot the percentage of participants affected against dose. This type of relationship is called:
explanation: Quantal dose-response curves describe the proportion of a population showing an all-or-none response (such as an adverse event) at each dose, from which ED50 and TD50 are derived. Graded curves instead measure the magnitude of effect in an individual. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Pharmacodynamics)
optionExplanations: Graded responses are continuous measures in a single subject, such as blood pressure change.
The therapeutic index is a ratio (TD50/ED50) derived from quantal curves, not the curve itself.
This plots effect against time at a fixed dose.
This relates drug concentration to receptor occupancy.

stem: Researchers recruit 100 patients with oral cancer and 100 age-matched controls without cancer, and ask all participants about previous betel quid use. Which study design is this, and which measure of association is appropriate?
explanation: Selecting participants by disease status (cases and controls) and looking back at exposure defines a case-control study. Since incidence cannot be calculated, the odds ratio is the measure of association. (First Aid — Biostatistics and Epidemiology: Study designs)
optionExplanations: A cohort study follows exposed and unexposed individuals forward to see who develops disease.
Cross-sectional studies sample a population at one point regardless of outcome status.
No intervention is assigned here.
A case series has no control group and no valid comparison.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with generalised anxiety disorder wishes to avoid a drug that causes sedation, dependence, or withdrawal. She is started on buspirone. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors
explanation: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist used for generalised anxiety disorder. It does not cause sedation, dependence, or respiratory depression, but it takes several weeks to act and does not help acute anxiety. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Anxiolytics)
optionExplanations: This is the mechanism of benzodiazepines, which cause sedation and dependence.
SSRIs block the serotonin transporter, unlike buspirone.
This describes propranolol, which reduces somatic anxiety symptoms.
This describes hydroxyzine, a sedating anxiolytic.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with moderate acne is started on doxycycline. Which describes the mechanism of action of tetracyclines?
options: Bind the 50S subunit and inhibit peptidyl transferase
Bind the 50S subunit and block translocation
Bind the 30S subunit and block formation of the initiation complex
Inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and block attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site
explanation: Tetracyclines are bacteriostatic and bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, preventing aminoacyl-tRNA from binding the A site. They chelate divalent cations and are contraindicated in pregnancy and in young children because of tooth discolouration. (First Aid — Pharmacology: Protein synthesis inhibitors)
optionExplanations: This is the mechanism of chloramphenicol.
This is the mechanism of macrolides and clindamycin.
This is the mechanism of aminoglycosides.
This is the mechanism of fluoroquinolones.

stem: A 30-year-old man is brought after a road traffic accident with heart rate 132/min, BP 80/50 mmHg, cold peripheries, and a distended abdomen with positive FAST. Haemoglobin on arrival is 6.5 g/dL. He has already received 1 L of warmed crystalloid with only a transient response. What is the most appropriate next step in fluid resuscitation?
options: Transfuse packed red cells (with balanced plasma and platelets as per a massive-transfusion protocol)
Give another litre of normal saline
Start vasopressors to raise blood pressure
explanation: In Class III-IV haemorrhagic shock, initial crystalloid is limited and patients who respond transiently or not at all need blood early. Blood components are given in a balanced ratio, and bleeding is controlled surgically. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Transfusion; Cardiovascular: Shock)
optionExplanations: Further crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy.
Dextrose distributes into total body water and does not restore intravascular volume.
Platelets alone do not restore oxygen-carrying capacity or volume.
Hypotension from haemorrhage requires blood replacement, not vasopressors, which would worsen perfusion.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent spontaneous right-sided nosebleeds, usually after nose picking. Examination shows crusting and a prominent vessel on the anterior septum. Which site is the most likely source of bleeding?
options: Woodruff plexus on the posterior lateral nasal wall
Little's area (Kiesselbach plexus) on the anterior nasal septum
Roof of the nose via the anterior ethmoidal artery
The nasopharynx, from a juvenile angiofibroma
explanation: Little's area on the anterior septum, where branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and superior labial arteries anastomose, is the commonest site of epistaxis in children and young adults, usually due to digital trauma. (First Aid — Anatomy: Head and neck vasculature)
optionExplanations: Woodruff plexus is a posterior bleeding site seen in older, hypertensive patients.
This is the site of posterior bleeding from the sphenopalatine artery.
Ethmoidal bleeding is usually traumatic or surgical.
Angiofibroma occurs in adolescent males with obstruction and profuse epistaxis.

stem: The tympanic membrane is a three-layered structure. Which combination correctly reflects the embryological origin of its outer, middle, and inner layers?
explanation: The tympanic membrane forms at the junction of the first pharyngeal cleft (ectoderm, outer epithelial layer) and the first pharyngeal pouch (endoderm, inner mucosal layer), with mesenchyme (mesoderm) forming the middle fibrous layer. (First Aid — Anatomy: Embryology, pharyngeal apparatus)
optionExplanations: The layers are reversed in this option: the outer layer is ectodermal.
The fibrous middle layer is derived from mesoderm and the inner mucosa from endoderm.
The skin-like outer layer cannot be mesodermal.
The inner mucosal layer is lined by endoderm of the first pharyngeal pouch.

stem: A child with Treacher Collins syndrome has conductive hearing loss due to first-arch maldevelopment. Which ossicles are derived from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel cartilage)?
explanation: The malleus and incus come from the first pharyngeal arch (Meckel cartilage), while the stapes, styloid process, and lesser horn of the hyoid come from the second arch (Reichert cartilage). (First Aid — Anatomy: Pharyngeal arch derivatives)
optionExplanations: The stapes is second-arch derived.
The stapes is a derivative of the second arch (Reichert cartilage).
The stapes is the only ossicle of second-arch origin, not first.
The stapes originates from the second arch.

stem: A 58-year-old man dies of an acute myocardial infarction. Autopsy shows an occlusive thrombus in the left anterior descending artery. Compared with a venous thrombus, this thrombus is most likely to be:
options: Red-cell rich with little fibrin, forming in static blood
A pure fibrin clot without platelets
Mostly composed of white blood cells with no fibrin
A fat embolus lodged in the coronary artery
Platelet-rich and pale, with prominent lines of Zahn
explanation: Arterial thrombi form at sites of endothelial injury or turbulent high-flow blood and are platelet-rich ('white'), with lines of Zahn. Venous thrombi form in stasis, contain more red cells, and are 'red' thrombi. (First Aid — Pathology: Thrombosis; Cardiovascular: Ischemic heart disease)
optionExplanations: Red thrombi are venous and form in areas of stasis.
Arterial thrombi form on injured endothelium and are platelet rich.
Leucocytes make up only a minor component.
Fat emboli do not cause typical coronary thrombosis.

stem: A 60-year-old man in the emergency department has crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw, with ST-elevation in leads V1-V4. Which one of the following initial interventions has been shown to reduce mortality independent of reperfusion therapy?
options: High-flow oxygen in a normoxic patient
explanation: In suspected ACS, immediate aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and thereby thromboxane A2, reducing mortality (ISIS-2). Nitrates and morphine are for symptom relief, and oxygen is only for hypoxaemia. (First Aid — Cardiovascular: Acute coronary syndromes)
optionExplanations: GTN relieves ischaemic pain but has not been shown to reduce mortality.
Morphine relieves pain and anxiety but is not shown to reduce mortality.
Routine oxygen in normoxic patients has no mortality benefit.
Prophylactic lidocaine increases mortality and is not recommended.

stem: A newborn who did not receive prophylaxis at birth presents on day 5 with umbilical stump bleeding and melaena. PT is prolonged. Which group of clotting factors is deficient in vitamin K deficiency?
explanation: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. Newborns are at risk because of low stores and sterile gut, and the PT rises first because factor VII has the shortest half-life. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Coagulation cascade)
optionExplanations: These factors are not vitamin K dependent.
These are intrinsic pathway factors, and only IX is vitamin K dependent.
Factors V and XI are not vitamin K dependent.
Fibrinogen, factor V and VIII are not vitamin K dependent.

stem: A 42-year-old man has fatigue, bruising, and pancytopenia. Marrow shows 45% myeloblasts, some with Auer rods that stain positive for myeloperoxidase. Cytogenetics do not show t(15;17). What is the standard induction chemotherapy?
options: Cytarabine for 7 days with an anthracycline (daunorubicin or idarubicin) for 3 days
Rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone (R-CHOP)
explanation: Myeloperoxidase-positive Auer rods identify AML. Standard induction is the '7+3' regimen of cytarabine for 7 days plus an anthracycline for 3 days. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Acute myelogenous leukemia)
optionExplanations: This is part of induction therapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
Imatinib treats CML and Philadelphia-positive disease.
R-CHOP treats B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
This regimen is used for CLL.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with bruising, fever, and bleeding gums. Labs show pancytopenia, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, and a marrow with abnormal promyelocytes containing numerous Auer rods. Karyotype shows t(15;17). Which treatment should be started immediately?
explanation: t(15;17) forms PML-RARA, which defines acute promyelocytic leukaemia. ATRA induces differentiation of the promyelocytes and is started on clinical suspicion, with arsenic trioxide, to prevent DIC-related haemorrhage. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Acute promyelocytic leukemia)
optionExplanations: Cytarabine alone is not the specific treatment, and delaying differentiating therapy risks fatal haemorrhage.
Imatinib targets BCR-ABL, which is absent here.
Cladribine is the drug used for hairy cell leukaemia.
Rituximab targets CD20 in B-cell lymphoma.

stem: A 14-year-old boy has tall stature, a marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, and downward dislocation of the lenses. He had a deep vein thrombosis last year. Urine homocysteine and plasma methionine are both raised. Which enzyme is deficient?
explanation: Homocystinuria due to cystathionine synthase deficiency (treated with B6, low methionine diet, and cysteine supplementation) causes marfanoid habitus, downward lens subluxation, thromboembolism, and intellectual disability. Methionine synthase and MTHFR defects raise homocysteine but not methionine. (First Aid — Biochemistry: Homocystinuria)
optionExplanations: Methionine synthase deficiency raises homocysteine but methionine is low.
This deficiency causes alkaptonuria, with dark urine and ochronosis.
This deficiency causes phenylketonuria, with musty odour and fair skin.
Cystathionase deficiency causes cystathioninuria, which is generally benign.

stem: A 50-year-old man with end-stage renal disease has bone pain and muscle weakness. Labs show low calcium, high phosphate, high potassium, high PTH, and low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. What is the primary mechanism of his bone disease?
options: Reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity and phosphate retention, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism
Excess vitamin D intake causing bone resorption
Parathyroid hormone resistance with undetectable PTH
explanation: In CKD, impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation lowers calcitriol, and phosphate is retained, leading to hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. This produces renal osteodystrophy (osteitis fibrosa cystica, rugger-jersey spine). (First Aid — Renal: Renal osteodystrophy)
optionExplanations: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia and low phosphate.
Vitamin D excess causes hypercalcaemia.
PTH is raised here, and pseudohypoparathyroidism has a different pattern.
Calcitonin does not account for secondary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has a slowly growing lateral neck mass. She has ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis, and CT shows a mass in the post-styloid parapharyngeal space. Which structure within this compartment is responsible for her Horner syndrome?
explanation: The post-styloid (retrostyloid) parapharyngeal space contains the carotid sheath (internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus), cranial nerves IX-XII, and the cervical sympathetic chain. Tumours here, such as paragangliomas and schwannomas, can cause Horner syndrome and lower cranial nerve palsies. (First Aid — Anatomy: Neck)
optionExplanations: CN XII injury causes tongue deviation, not Horner syndrome.
The facial nerve is not in this space and would cause facial paralysis.
Compression of the vein does not produce an oculosympathetic palsy.
CN IX injury causes pharyngeal sensory loss and an absent gag reflex.

stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy. On day 2 she develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm. Which vessel was most likely damaged, compromising the blood supply of the parathyroid glands?
explanation: The parathyroid glands, both superior and inferior, are mainly supplied by the inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk). Devascularisation or removal after thyroidectomy causes hypocalcaemia, with perioral paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm. (First Aid — Endocrine: Parathyroid anatomy and hypocalcemia)
optionExplanations: The superior thyroid artery mainly supplies the upper thyroid pole and the superior parathyroids are variably supplied by it.
The thyroidea ima is an inconstant vessel and not the main parathyroid supply.
Injury would cause major haemorrhage and not selective parathyroid devascularisation.
This vessel is not related to the parathyroids.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has hoarseness after a total thyroidectomy. Laryngoscopy shows that the left vocal cord is fixed in the paramedian position. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: External branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
Left vagus nerve above the superior laryngeal nerve
explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid. Unilateral injury causes hoarseness with a paramedian cord, due to the unopposed cricothyroid, whereas bilateral injury can cause stridor. (First Aid — Anatomy: Larynx and vagus nerve branches)
optionExplanations: This nerve supplies the cricothyroid, and injury causes a weak, monotone voice with the cord at a normal position.
This nerve is sensory to the supraglottic larynx and does not move the cord.
A high vagal lesion would leave the cord in an intermediate (cadaveric) position.
This nerve controls tongue movement.

stem: After thyroid surgery, a professional singer notices that she can no longer reach high notes and her voice tires easily, although it is not hoarse and the vocal cords move normally. Which structure was injured?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords for high pitch. It runs close to the superior thyroid artery, and injury during ligation causes loss of pitch range and voice fatigue. (First Aid — Anatomy: Larynx)
optionExplanations: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness with an immobile cord.
This is a sensory nerve, and its injury risks aspiration but does not change pitch.
This would affect tongue movement.
This is not at risk in thyroid surgery.

stem: A 38-year-old teacher has had a persistent sore throat and mild hoarseness for 4 months, worse by the end of the school day. Laryngoscopy shows diffusely congested, thickened vocal cords with no discrete nodules, polyps or ulcers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chronic laryngitis follows chronic irritants such as voice abuse, smoking, reflux or dust, and shows diffuse congestion and thickening of the cords. Persistent hoarseness in smokers needs biopsy to exclude carcinoma, but the described scenario and findings suit simple chronic laryngitis. (First Aid — Respiratory: Upper airway disorders)
optionExplanations: Carcinoma is a ulceroproliferative or fixed lesion usually in smokers.
Nodules are discrete bilateral lesions at the junction of the anterior third and posterior two-thirds.
Papillomatosis shows wart-like lesions and affects children or young adults.
Vocal cord palsy shows a cord that fails to move on phonation.

stem: A 35-year-old man feels a sudden 'gunshot' in his calf while sprinting. The Thompson (calf squeeze) test produces no plantar flexion. Which muscles are attached to the calcaneus via the tendon that has ruptured?
options: Tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus
Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus
explanation: The Achilles tendon is formed by the gastrocnemius and soleus (with plantaris contributing) and inserts onto the posterior calcaneus. Rupture produces a palpable gap and a positive Thompson test. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal: Lower limb muscles)
optionExplanations: These tendons pass behind the medial malleolus and do not insert on the calcaneus.
These tendons pass behind the lateral malleolus to the foot.
These are dorsiflexors on the anterior compartment.
Popliteus unlocks the knee and does not insert on the calcaneus.

stem: A patient with a posterior interosseous nerve injury can still supinate his forearm with the elbow flexed. Which muscle and nerve account for the preserved supination?
options: Brachialis, supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
Pronator teres, supplied by the median nerve
Biceps brachii, supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
Brachioradialis, supplied by the radial nerve
Anconeus, supplied by the radial nerve
explanation: The supinator (a PIN-supplied muscle) is the main supinator in extension, but the biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator with the elbow flexed. The biceps is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, so supination is partly preserved in PIN palsy. (First Aid — Anatomy: Upper limb muscles and nerves)
optionExplanations: Brachialis flexes the elbow and does not supinate.
Pronator teres is a pronator.
Brachioradialis brings the forearm to a mid-position and is spared in PIN lesions, but it is not the major supinator.
Anconeus extends the elbow.

stem: A 60-year-old man has a leukoplakic lesion on the free edge of the true vocal cord, and a biopsy is taken. Which epithelium normally lines the true vocal cords?
explanation: The true vocal folds are lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium that tolerates the mechanical stress of phonation. Most of the rest of the larynx has respiratory-type pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. (First Aid — Respiratory: Larynx histology)
optionExplanations: This lines most of the larynx above and below the vocal folds.
Keratinised epithelium is abnormal here and suggests leukoplakia or keratosis.
This lines small ducts, not the vocal folds.
Transitional epithelium is found in the urinary tract.

stem: A patient swallows a fish bone that lodges in the piriform fossa. Which structure forms the medial wall of the piriform fossa?
options: Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
explanation: The piriform fossa lies on either side of the laryngeal inlet. Its medial wall is formed by the aryepiglottic fold (with the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages below) and its lateral wall by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. (First Aid — Anatomy: Pharynx and larynx)
optionExplanations: The thyroid lamina forms the lateral wall.
The thyrohyoid membrane contributes to the lateral wall.
This is a skeletal landmark and not the medial wall.
This muscle lies behind the cricoid lamina, not in the wall of the fossa.

stem: A 65-year-old man with herpes zoster ophthalmicus has vesicles at the tip of his nose (Hutchinson sign). Involvement of which nerve branch makes ocular complications likely?
options: Nasociliary nerve (V1), via its external nasal branch
explanation: The tip and dorsum of the external nose are supplied by the external nasal branch of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, a branch of the nasociliary nerve (V1). The same nerve supplies the cornea via the long ciliary nerves, so a nasal tip lesion predicts corneal involvement. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Trigeminal nerve)
optionExplanations: The infraorbital nerve supplies the lateral nose and cheek, and its involvement does not predict ocular disease.
The lacrimal nerve supplies the lacrimal gland and lateral upper lid, not the tip of the nose.
The supraorbital nerve supplies the forehead and scalp.
This supplies the cheek prominence.

stem: Which of the following arteries supplying the anterior nasal septum is a branch of the internal carotid artery system?
options: Anterior ethmoidal artery (from the ophthalmic artery)
explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries arise from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system) and supply the anterosuperior nasal cavity. The rest of the nasal blood supply, including the sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and superior labial arteries, comes from the external carotid. (First Aid — Anatomy: Nasal blood supply)
optionExplanations: This is a terminal branch of the maxillary artery (external carotid).
This is a branch of the maxillary artery (external carotid).
This is a branch of the facial artery (external carotid).
This is a branch of the sphenopalatine artery (external carotid).

stem: Sensation from the mucosa of the piriform fossa travels through which nerve?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus)
explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve (branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the vagus) pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and supplies sensation to the larynx above the vocal folds and the piriform fossa. Injury leads to aspiration. (First Aid — Anatomy: Vagus nerve branches)
optionExplanations: The external branch is motor to the cricothyroid.
This supplies the larynx below the vocal folds.
This supplies the oropharynx and posterior tongue.
This is a motor nerve to the tongue.

stem: After a middle-ear operation, a patient complains of a metallic taste and loss of taste sensation over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but general sensation of the tongue is normal. Which nerve was injured?
explanation: The chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands. It crosses the middle ear between the malleus and incus, making it vulnerable during ear surgery. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Cranial nerve VII)
optionExplanations: The lingual nerve carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, which is intact.
This nerve carries taste from the posterior third.
This carries secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland and nasal glands.
This is motor to the tongue.

stem: At approximately what age does the frontal sinus first become visible on a plain radiograph?
explanation: The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth, the sphenoid develops by about 3 years, and the frontal sinus first becomes radiographically visible at about 6-7 years, reaching adult size after puberty. (First Aid — Anatomy: Paranasal sinuses)
optionExplanations: Only the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth; the frontal sinus is not yet pneumatised.
The frontal sinus is still a cell in the frontal bone at this age.
Pneumatisation of the frontal sinus is not yet radiologically visible by age 3.
It has largely developed by this age and is visible earlier.

stem: A 5-year-old boy has a pruritic vesicular eruption in successive crops, with lesions at different stages (macules, vesicles, crusts) on the trunk. After recovery, in which site does the causative virus remain latent?
options: Dorsal root and cranial nerve sensory ganglia
Mononuclear cells of the bone marrow
explanation: The picture is varicella ('dewdrop on a rose petal' vesicles in different stages). VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia and reactivates as herpes zoster, which is a dermatomal vesicular eruption. (First Aid — Microbiology: Herpesviruses)
optionExplanations: Bone marrow monocytes are a latency site for cytomegalovirus.
B cells are a latency site for Epstein-Barr virus.
These are not a latency site for VZV.
Hepatocytes harbour hepatitis B DNA, not VZV.

stem: In a patient with an intact tympanic membrane, tubal function is assessed by asking him to swallow while his nostrils are closed, and the movement of the drum is observed. This test is known as:
explanation: The Toynbee test assesses Eustachian tube patency using swallowing against a closed nose, which creates negative pressure in the middle ear. Valsalva uses positive pressure, and Politzer uses an air bag. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Ear)
optionExplanations: Valsalva is forced expiration against closed nose and mouth, producing positive pressure.
This inflates the Eustachian tube using a Politzer bag.
The Rinne test compares air and bone conduction with a tuning fork.
This test assesses stapes mobility with pressure changes in the canal.

stem: Which is the largest and most constant air cell of the anterior ethmoid sinuses, forming a prominent landmark in endoscopic sinus surgery?
explanation: The ethmoid bulla is the largest, most constant anterior ethmoid cell, lying below the basal lamella of the middle turbinate and bounding the hiatus semilunaris. It is a key landmark in functional endoscopic sinus surgery. (First Aid — Anatomy: Paranasal sinuses)
optionExplanations: The agger nasi is the most anterior ethmoid cell, lying in front of the middle turbinate attachment.
Haller cells are infraorbital ethmoid cells below the orbit.
Onodi cells are posterior ethmoid cells extending lateral to the sphenoid sinus.
A concha bullosa is an aerated middle turbinate, not an ethmoid air cell.

stem: A 25-year-old man has a painful, red, tender swelling at the tip of the nose after picking his nose. It is a furuncle at the nasal vestibule. Which complication is most feared?
options: Brain abscess from direct bony erosion
Septal perforation from ischaemia of the septum
explanation: Nasal vestibular furuncle (Staphylococcus aureus) can spread via the valveless angular and facial veins to the ophthalmic veins and the cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis. The central face is called the 'danger triangle', and manipulation of lesions here should be avoided. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Cavernous sinus)
optionExplanations: Rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis, not nasal furuncles.
Spread is through venous channels, not direct bony erosion.
This is not the typical life-threatening complication.
This is not a complication of a furuncle.

stem: During septoplasty, what is the minimum width of dorsal and caudal septal cartilage (L-strut) that should be preserved to prevent collapse and saddle deformity of the nose?
options: 0 mm, since the dorsum is supported by nasal bones
explanation: A dorsal and caudal L-strut of at least 10 mm of septal cartilage should be preserved in septoplasty to maintain tip support and prevent saddle nose deformity or columellar retraction. (First Aid — Anatomy: Nasal septum)
optionExplanations: This is too thin and would not support the nasal dorsum or tip.
This is below the recommended safe minimum.
This is more than required, and conservative resection of that magnitude is not needed.
The cartilaginous dorsum and caudal strut support the nasal tip, so preservation is required.

stem: A healthy 20-year-old man complains that the side of his nose that is blocked alternates every few hours. Examination of the nose is normal. What is the explanation?
explanation: The nasal cycle is a normal alternation of congestion and decongestion of the turbinates (erectile tissue under autonomic control), seen in most healthy people. The total nasal airflow remains constant. (First Aid — Respiratory: Nasal physiology)
optionExplanations: Allergic rhinitis causes bilateral congestion, sneezing and watery rhinorrhoea.
A septal deviation causes a fixed unilateral obstruction.
Polyps cause persistent obstruction that does not alternate.
This occurs after overuse of topical decongestants and affects both sides.

stem: A 22-year-old woman has sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, and itchy eyes each spring. A nasal smear is most likely to show an increase in which cell type?
explanation: Seasonal allergic rhinitis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction, and nasal smears and mucosa show eosinophils with IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation. (First Aid — Immunology: Hypersensitivity)
optionExplanations: Neutrophils predominate in bacterial rhinosinusitis.
Lymphocytes predominate in viral infections.
Plasma cells are not a feature of the nasal smear in allergy.
Macrophages are not the characteristic cell in allergic rhinitis smears.

stem: A 35-year-old long-distance truck driver treated for allergic rhinitis complains of drowsiness. Which antihistamine is most likely to be the cause?
explanation: First-generation H1 blockers (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine) are lipophilic, cross the blood-brain barrier, and cause sedation and anticholinergic effects. Second-generation agents (loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine) are far less sedating. (First Aid — Pharmacology: H1 blockers)
optionExplanations: Loratadine is a second-generation H1 blocker that does not cross the blood-brain barrier appreciably.
Fexofenadine is non-sedating.
This is a second-generation non-sedating drug.
Montelukast is a leukotriene receptor antagonist and not an antihistamine.

stem: A 72-year-old hypertensive man has profuse epistaxis flowing down the throat. Anterior and posterior nasal packing has failed to stop the bleeding. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Silver nitrate cautery of the anterior septum
Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery cautery or ligation
explanation: Posterior epistaxis usually arises from the sphenopalatine artery territory. When packing fails, the next step is endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or cautery, with arterial embolisation as an alternative. (First Aid — Respiratory: Epistaxis)
optionExplanations: Packing has already failed.
This is for identifiable anterior bleeding vessels.
This is not a treatment for epistaxis.
Tranexamic acid is an adjunct and will not control brisk arterial bleeding.

stem: A craniofacial surgeon wants to know which arteries mainly supply the temporalis muscle. They are:
options: Deep temporal arteries from the maxillary artery
explanation: Temporalis is supplied mainly by the anterior and posterior deep temporal arteries (branches of the maxillary artery), with a contribution from the middle temporal artery. Its nerve supply is the deep temporal nerves from V3. (First Aid — Anatomy: Muscles of mastication)
optionExplanations: The facial artery supplies the face and not the temporalis.
These supply the nasal cavity.
The lingual artery supplies the tongue.
This artery supplies the pharynx and not the temporalis.

stem: A 15-year-old obese girl has velvety, hyperpigmented, thickened plaques over the nape of the neck and axillae. Which investigation is the most appropriate next step?
options: HbA1c (or fasting glucose) to screen for diabetes or insulin resistance
explanation: Acanthosis nigricans reflects hyperinsulinaemia stimulating keratinocyte proliferation through IGF-1 receptors. It is a marker of insulin resistance and diabetes risk, so HbA1c or fasting glucose should be measured. Rarely, it is a paraneoplastic sign of gastric adenocarcinoma. (First Aid — Endocrine: Diabetes mellitus; Musculoskeletal, Skin, and Connective Tissue: Acanthosis nigricans)
optionExplanations: The clinical picture is typical of acanthosis nigricans, which requires screening for insulin resistance rather than biopsy.
ANA is not indicated here.
Vitamin D is not related to these lesions.
Scrapings are for tinea.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has progressive bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus that worsened during pregnancy. Otoscopy is normal. Pure-tone audiometry shows a conductive hearing loss, with a dip in the bone conduction threshold at 2000 Hz (Carhart notch). What is the most likely diagnosis?
