explanation: Otosclerosis causes stapes footplate fixation, resulting in a progressive conductive hearing loss, often worse in pregnancy, with a Carhart notch (apparent bone conduction dip at 2000 Hz) on audiometry. Noise-induced loss produces a notch at 4000 Hz. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Hearing loss)
optionExplanations: Meniere disease causes fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss with vertigo.
Presbycusis is a high-frequency sensorineural loss in older people.
This shows a notch at 4000 Hz in sensorineural loss.
Acoustic neuroma causes unilateral sensorineural loss.

stem: Tympanometry in a patient with a normal-looking eardrum shows a type As curve (shallow compliance peak at normal middle-ear pressure). Which condition is most likely?
explanation: The type As tympanogram indicates a stiff middle-ear system with reduced compliance but normal pressure, characteristic of otosclerosis or ossicular fixation. Type B suggests fluid or perforation, type C eustachian tube dysfunction, and type Ad ossicular discontinuity. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Ear)
optionExplanations: Effusion produces a flat type B curve.
This produces a type C curve with negative pressure.
Discontinuity produces a type Ad curve with abnormally high compliance.
A normal ear gives a type A curve with normal peak compliance.

stem: Damage to the piriform cortex and periamygdaloid area, the primary olfactory cortex, would most directly impair which sensory function, and what is unusual about its pathway?
options: Vision; it relays in the lateral geniculate nucleus
Hearing; it relays in the medial geniculate body
Taste; it relays in the ventral posteromedial nucleus
Smell; it reaches the cortex without first relaying in the thalamus
Touch; it relays in the ventral posterolateral nucleus
explanation: Olfactory receptor axons synapse in the olfactory bulb, and the lateral olfactory tract projects directly to the piriform cortex, periamygdaloid cortex, and entorhinal cortex, with no thalamic relay. This is unique among the senses. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Olfactory pathway)
optionExplanations: Vision is processed in the occipital cortex after relay in the lateral geniculate body.
Auditory pathway projects to the temporal cortex via the medial geniculate.
Taste relays through VPM to the insula and operculum.
Touch relays through VPL to the postcentral gyrus.

stem: A 68-year-old man who has had a right posterior cerebral artery infarct can no longer recognise his wife by her face, although he immediately knows who she is when she speaks, and he can read, name objects and recognise familiar rituals. Which area is most likely damaged?
options: Angular gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
explanation: Prosopagnosia (inability to recognise faces) results from damage to the fusiform face area of the inferior temporo-occipital cortex, classically bilateral or right-sided. Recognition by voice remains intact since auditory pathways are spared. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Cerebral cortex lesions)
optionExplanations: Angular gyrus lesions cause Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation).
This area is involved in auditory processing and Wernicke language comprehension.
The amygdala is involved in emotional processing, and its lesion causes Kluver-Bucy syndrome.
This region is involved in executive function.

stem: With his eyes closed, a patient cannot recognise a number traced on his palm (impaired graphaesthesia). Which ascending tract carries this sensation from the periphery to the brainstem?
explanation: Fine touch, vibration, two-point discrimination, and proprioception ascend through the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus), synapse in the nucleus gracilis/cuneatus, decussate as internal arcuate fibres, and ascend in the medial lemniscus to the VPL nucleus. Graphaesthesia is also interpreted by the parietal cortex. (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Spinal cord tracts)
optionExplanations: This tract carries pain and temperature.
This tract carries crude touch and pressure.
This tract carries unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum.
This is a descending motor pathway.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent unexpected episodes of palpitations, sweating, and fear of dying, which peak within 10 minutes. Neurobiological models of her disorder implicate hyperactivity of which brainstem nucleus and neurotransmitter?
explanation: Panic disorder is linked to dysregulation of the locus coeruleus (the main source of norepinephrine) and its noradrenergic discharge, along with serotonergic and GABAergic dysfunction. SSRIs and cognitive behavioural therapy are first-line treatments. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Panic disorder; Neurotransmitter changes)
optionExplanations: The raphe nuclei are the source of serotonin and are implicated in depression.
The VTA is the origin of mesolimbic dopamine projections involved in reward and psychosis.
This nucleus degenerates in Alzheimer disease.
Degeneration of the substantia nigra underlies Parkinson disease.

stem: A 24-year-old man has auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions along with flat affect, poverty of speech, and social withdrawal. Which pairing of dopamine pathways best explains his positive and negative symptoms?
options: Nigrostriatal dopamine excess (positive symptoms) and tuberoinfundibular deficiency (negative symptoms)
Mesocortical dopamine excess (positive symptoms) and mesolimbic deficiency (negative symptoms)
Mesolimbic dopamine excess (positive symptoms) and mesocortical dopamine deficiency (negative symptoms)
Tuberoinfundibular dopamine excess (positive symptoms) and nigrostriatal deficiency (negative symptoms)
Serotonin excess in the raphe nuclei (positive symptoms) and dopamine excess in the nucleus accumbens (negative symptoms)
explanation: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway (positive symptoms) and reduced activity in the mesocortical pathway (negative and cognitive symptoms). Antipsychotics block D2 receptors and treat positive symptoms better than negative ones. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Schizophrenia)
optionExplanations: Nigrostriatal dysfunction is responsible for extrapyramidal side effects, not psychosis.
The pathways are reversed in this option.
The tuberoinfundibular pathway controls prolactin release.
This option does not describe the accepted dopamine hypothesis.

stem: Which brain structure, receiving dopaminergic projections from the ventral tegmental area, is the key centre of the brain's reward circuit and is activated by addictive drugs such as cocaine?
explanation: The mesolimbic dopamine pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum), the core of the brain reward system, and it mediates reinforcement in addiction. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Substance use disorders; Neurology: Basal ganglia)
optionExplanations: The hippocampus is involved in memory consolidation.
The locus coeruleus is a noradrenergic nucleus involved in arousal and panic.
The vermis regulates truncal balance and coordination.
These are part of the Papez circuit for memory, damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic alcohol use presents with confusion, ataxia and nystagmus, and later with severe anterograde amnesia and confabulation. Which lesion best explains his memory deficit?
explanation: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome follows thiamine deficiency and damages the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus. Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) is treated with IV thiamine before glucose, while Korsakoff syndrome produces irreversible anterograde amnesia with confabulation. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Alcohol use; Neurology: Wernicke-Korsakoff)
optionExplanations: Caudate atrophy is seen in Huntington disease.
Vermian degeneration explains the ataxia but not the amnesia.
Loss here is seen in Alzheimer disease.
A lesion here causes contralateral hemiballismus.

stem: An agitated 30-year-old man with schizophrenia is on a mood stabiliser plus an antipsychotic. His aggression has settled, but he now cannot sleep, feels an inner restlessness, and constantly paces the ward. There is no rigidity or tremor. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Subjective inner restlessness and pacing after starting an antipsychotic is akathisia. Treatment options include reducing the dose or switching the drug, and adding a beta blocker (propranolol), a benzodiazepine, or mirtazapine. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Antipsychotic adverse effects)
optionExplanations: Raising the dose of the offending antipsychotic will worsen the akathisia.
Another dopamine blocker would likely worsen akathisia.
The mood stabiliser is not the likely cause of the restlessness.
Anticholinergics are first-line for dystonia and parkinsonism, and are less effective in akathisia.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is confused and tearful, repeatedly asking 'Where am I?'. On testing she is unable to copy a drawing of two intersecting pentagons, although her language is fluent. Which brain region is mainly responsible for the task she fails?
explanation: Constructional apraxia, an inability to copy figures such as intersecting pentagons (a component of the MMSE), reflects parietal lobe (particularly non-dominant) dysfunction. It is common in Alzheimer disease and other dementias. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Delirium and dementia; Neurology: Cortical lesions)
optionExplanations: The occipital lobe is the primary visual cortex, and damage causes visual field defects.
The temporal lobe is involved in memory and auditory processing.
The cerebellum coordinates movement and does not govern visuospatial construction.
The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis, appetite, and circadian rhythm.

stem: A 40-year-old woman on amitriptyline for depression has gained 8 kg and feels very sleepy during the day. Which receptor action is mainly responsible for these side effects?
explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants block H1 receptors, causing sedation and weight gain, M1 receptors (anticholinergic effects), alpha-1 receptors (orthostasis), and cardiac sodium channels (arrhythmias). (First Aid — Psychiatry: Tricyclic antidepressants)
optionExplanations: Muscarinic blockade causes dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and blurred vision.
Alpha-1 blockade causes orthostatic hypotension and dizziness.
This is responsible for cardiotoxicity (QRS widening) in overdose.
TCAs have minimal D2 activity.

stem: A 35-year-old man with depression has improved after 2 months of treatment but now reports delayed ejaculation and reduced libido. Which antidepressant is most likely to be responsible?
explanation: SSRIs are the antidepressants most commonly associated with sexual dysfunction, including decreased libido, anorgasmia and delayed ejaculation, due to increased serotonin. Management includes dose reduction, a drug holiday, switching, or adding bupropion. (First Aid — Psychiatry: SSRIs)
optionExplanations: Bupropion has little sexual dysfunction and is used to counter SSRI sexual side effects.
Mirtazapine has a low rate of sexual side effects.
Trazodone causes sedation and rarely priapism, and has a relatively low incidence of delayed ejaculation.
Lithium is a mood stabiliser, not a typical cause of ejaculatory delay.

stem: A 45-year-old man on sertraline has insomnia, and his doctor adds a low-dose sedating antidepressant at bedtime. A week later he presents with a painful erection lasting 5 hours. Which drug is the most likely cause?
explanation: Trazodone, an antidepressant with alpha-1 adrenergic blockade, is used as a hypnotic and can cause priapism. This is a urological emergency requiring aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine. (First Aid — Psychiatry: Atypical antidepressants)
optionExplanations: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is not usually linked to priapism.
Mirtazapine causes weight gain and sedation and is not typically linked to priapism.
Buspirone is an anxiolytic and does not cause priapism.
Venlafaxine causes hypertension and sexual dysfunction.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has painless generalised lymphadenopathy that has waxed and waned for 2 years. Lymph node biopsy shows a nodular pattern of small cleaved cells expressing CD10 and CD20. Which genetic abnormality is characteristic of this lymphoma?
options: t(11;14) with overexpression of cyclin D1
explanation: Follicular lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm of centrocytes and centroblasts, with t(14;18) placing BCL-2 under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain promoter. BCL-2 overexpression blocks apoptosis, so the disease is indolent and waxes and wanes. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma)
optionExplanations: This translocation is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma.
This translocation is characteristic of mantle cell lymphoma.
The Philadelphia chromosome is characteristic of CML.
This translocation is characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

stem: A 25-year-old man has painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, drenching night sweats, and pruritus. A lymph node biopsy shows binucleated cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli (owl-eye appearance). What is the characteristic immunophenotype of these cells?
options: CD20 positive, CD10 positive, CD15 negative
CD15 positive, CD30 positive, CD45 negative
CD3 positive, CD4 positive, CD30 negative
CD5 positive, CD23 positive, CD20 weakly positive
explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma are CD15 and CD30 positive and CD45 negative, and are of B-cell origin. The nodular sclerosis subtype is commonest, and the disease is staged by the Ann Arbor system. (First Aid — Hematology and Oncology: Hodgkin lymphoma)
optionExplanations: This is the phenotype of follicular lymphoma and other B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
This is a T-cell phenotype and does not fit Reed-Sternberg cells.
This is the phenotype of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
This is the phenotype of plasma cells in multiple myeloma.

stem: Which event controls progression of the cell cycle through the G1/S restriction point?
options: Binding of p53 to the Rb promoter
Phosphorylation of Rb by cyclin D-CDK4/6, releasing E2F
Degradation of cyclin E-CDK2 by p27
explanation: In G1, mitogenic signals induce cyclin D, which with CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb. Hyperphosphorylated Rb releases E2F, which drives transcription of genes for S phase entry. p53 (through p21) and p16 inhibit this checkpoint. (First Aid — Pathology: Cell cycle regulation)
optionExplanations: This complex drives entry into mitosis (G2/M transition).
p53 acts mainly by inducing p21, which blocks CDKs, not by directly activating the restriction point.
Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F and arrests the cycle at G1.
p27 inhibits cyclin E-CDK2 and halts the cycle.

stem: A patient with a myocardial infarction feels pain in the left arm, and a patient with a gallbladder inflammation feels pain at the tip of the right shoulder. Which mechanism best explains referred pain?
options: Direct cross-over of visceral pain fibres to somatic nerves in the periphery
Retrograde transmission of pain along sympathetic efferents
Release of substance P from the dorsal root ganglia into the bloodstream
Convergence of visceral and somatic afferent fibres from the same spinal segment on common dorsal horn neurons
Direct stimulation of cutaneous nociceptors by the diseased organ
explanation: Visceral and somatic afferents from the same dermatome converge on the same second-order spinothalamic neurons in the dorsal horn, and the brain interprets the visceral input as arising from the somatic area (convergence-projection theory). (First Aid — Neurology and Special Senses: Pain pathways)
optionExplanations: There is no peripheral cross-over of nerve fibres.
Referred pain is not due to efferent conduction.
Referred pain is a neural, not humoral, phenomenon.
The organ is not in contact with the skin.

stem: A 17-year-old boy has vague pain around the umbilicus that later localises to the right iliac fossa. At which spinal segment level is the early visceral pain of appendicitis referred?
explanation: Visceral afferents from the appendix (midgut) travel with sympathetic fibres to enter the cord at T10, so early appendicitis is felt in the T10 dermatome (periumbilical). Later irritation of the parietal peritoneum localises pain to the right iliac fossa. (First Aid — Gastrointestinal: Referred pain)
optionExplanations: T6 corresponds to the epigastric region.
T8 corresponds to the upper epigastrium.
T12 corresponds to the suprapubic region.
L4 corresponds to the anterior thigh and knee region.

stem: A person feels the urge to defecate when the rectum is distended with faeces. Through which nerves are these sensations carried?
explanation: Rectal stretch sensation (urge to defecate) is carried by visceral afferents in the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4), which also carry parasympathetic efferents. The pudendal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter and the anal canal below the pectinate line. (First Aid — Anatomy: Pelvic innervation)
optionExplanations: Hypogastric nerves carry sympathetic fibres and sensation from the fundus of the uterus and the peritoneal-covered parts.
The pudendal nerve carries somatic sensation from the anal canal below the pectinate line and supplies the external anal sphincter.
These carry sympathetic fibres to the inferior mesenteric ganglion.
These carry sympathetic fibres to the aorticorenal ganglion.

stem: After a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus, a 12-year-old boy has a claw-like deformity of the ring and little fingers, inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joints of these fingers, and sensory loss over the medial one-and-a-half fingers and the hypothenar eminence. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle and supplies the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus, the hypothenar muscles, the interossei, and the medial two lumbricals, with sensation to the medial 1.5 digits. Injury at the elbow gives clawing and positive Froment sign. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal: Upper limb nerve injuries)
optionExplanations: Median nerve injury causes thenar wasting, a 'hand of benediction', and sensory loss over the lateral three and a half digits.
Radial nerve injury causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the first web space.
This is a purely motor nerve that causes weakness of the index and thumb flexion (OK sign).
This nerve supplies the flexors of the arm and sensation to the lateral forearm.

stem: A 40-year-old man sustains a dislocation of the radial head. He cannot extend his fingers or thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joints, but he can still extend his wrist (with radial deviation) and has no sensory loss. Which nerve is injured?
options: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of the radial nerve) pierces the supinator at the arcade of Frohse and supplies the finger and thumb extensors and the supinator. It is purely motor, and extensor carpi radialis longus is spared, so wrist extension is preserved with radial deviation. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal: Upper limb nerve injuries)
optionExplanations: A lesion at the spiral groove gives wrist drop and sensory loss.
This nerve is a branch of the median nerve and causes loss of pinch grip.
This nerve is purely sensory.
Ulnar injury causes clawing and sensory loss in the medial hand.

stem: A 25-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand and has pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. The initial wrist X-ray appears normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure him that there is no fracture and discharge
Early mobilisation with a simple crepe bandage
Immediate surgical exploration of the wrist
Immobilise in a thumb spica cast and repeat imaging or obtain MRI
explanation: Snuffbox tenderness after FOOSH is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise, even with normal initial X-rays. Management is thumb spica immobilisation, and repeat X-rays after 10-14 days or MRI to confirm. (First Aid — Musculoskeletal: Upper limb fractures)
optionExplanations: Initial radiographs can miss scaphoid fractures, and missed fractures risk non-union and avascular necrosis.
This would risk displacement and non-union of an occult fracture.
Surgery is not indicated for suspected undisplaced fractures.
Injections would not treat a fracture.

stem: A 30-year-old man had a fracture through the waist of the scaphoid that was missed. Three months later he has persistent wrist pain, and X-ray shows sclerosis and fragmentation of the proximal pole. What is the mechanism of this complication?
options: Compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Septic arthritis of the radiocarpal joint
Damage to the anterior interosseous artery
Primary bone tumour of the carpus
